01What was asked forScope

Three deliverables, one system behind them.

Everything here comes out of a single decision about what Graffs is: a platform whose agents don’t just report, they act — and every action arrives with the route that produced it. Graffs’ own architecture calls that goal never silently wrong; stated as a promise, it’s no silent failures. The mark, the deck and the asset set are three expressions of it, which is why they hold together.

Deliverable 01

A logo that encapsulates the essence of Graffs

A G plotted between eight lattice points, with a node at every intersection.

Deliverable 02

A PowerPoint template aligned with the identity

Thirteen layouts, native charts, speaker notes on every slide.

Deliverable 03

Assets ready for immediate use

Vector and raster exports, favicons, the iOS app icon, the social image, both typefaces.

02The ideaGRF-BD-00

The name is the thesis.

Graffs sounds like graphs, and the product is one — a knowledge graph that models an operation as points joined by edges, which its agents traverse from a raw signal to a dispatched work order. So the mark isn’t a picture of the company. It’s the thing the company does, drawn once.

The letterform isn’t drawn. It’s plotted. A route between eight lattice points, with a node at every intersection — the way the product plots a reading. Anyone can rebuild it from the coordinate table below, which is the test a plotted mark passes and a drawn one doesn’t.

It carries two industries without changing. To a reliability engineer it’s an asset graph; to a safety officer it’s the graph tying a signal to the evidence behind it. The healthcare edition changes the ontology, not the identity.

Ink carries the edges. Oxide carries the points. Nothing else in the identity is allowed to.

03The lineGRF-BD-08

No silent failures.

The line doesn’t claim the system is always right. It claims something narrower and far harder: that when it’s wrong, you will know. That’s a promise about a failure mode rather than about quality, which is why it survives contact with an engineer.

Why not accuracy

Every platform in this category promises the outcome. A claim about how good something is can’t be checked; a claim about how it fails can. Testable is the only kind an engineer believes.

Why these words

Silent failure is a term of art in reliability engineering — the language a reliability engineer already uses in a standup, and one a safety officer reads the same way.

Why it’s short

Three words, set at display size in a lockup, on a slide, on a wall. Anything needing a subordinate clause is a sentence, not a line.

What changed
Never silently wrong
No silent failures

Graffs’ own architecture page sets the goal as never silently wrong. The promise is right; the wording spends its last word on a verdict. Failures names the thing that happens, where wrong passes judgement on it — and it stops asking the reader to picture the product being wrong in order to follow the claim.

Setting

Geologica Regular, sentence case, full stop. Never qualified — no virtually, no near, no asterisk. A promise with a modifier on it isn’t a promise.

04The markGRF-M-01

Construction

Rectangular lattice, five columns by eleven rows. 1ux = 0.43H, 1uy = 0.10H, where H is the height of the lattice itself. Every vertex sits on an intersection — no half-steps, no optical adjustments.

IDCoordRole
01x5, y3terminal, front
02x3, y1apex
03x1, y3shoulder
04x1, y9heel
05x3, y11base
06x5, y9tail
07x5, y6bar, outer
08x3, y6bar, inner
The aperture is 3u, matched by the tail run directly beneath it. It’s the mark’s only asymmetry and the reason it reads as a G rather than a ring. It’s never reduced.

At 24 px the nodes are still separate points. Below it they merge into the stroke — which is why the reduction alternate exists, and why it’s a different file rather than a scaled one.

05RulesGRF-M-02

Five rules. Everything else is preference.

  1. Stroke and nodeThe edge stroke is 0.12H. The node diameter is 1.7t. There’s no other node size, and no node colour other than oxide or the edge colour.
  2. The aperture3 lattice units, matched by the tail run below it. Never reduced — it’s the only thing stopping the mark reading as a closed ring.
  3. Below 24 pxDrop the nodes and step the stroke to 0.17H. Use the reduction alternate. Never shrink the full mark past this point.
  4. Clear spaceOne node diameter on every side, measured from the outer edge of the corner nodes. In the lockup, the gap between mark and wordmark is 4 lattice units.
  5. OxideOrange means a point is off its lattice, right now. Where a surface reports — a console, a chart, a status page, a dashboard — oxide arrives when a point deviates and leaves when it returns. Where a surface reports nothing — the mark, an icon, a cover, a decal, a booth wall, a printed object — it may be permanent, and may fill the whole ground. The test: could someone look at this to find out how something is doing? If yes, orange is temporary.
Clear space
06AlternatesGRF-M-03

A logo for every occasion.

Each exists for a situation the primary mark can’t cover. Where a situation isn’t listed here, the answer is the primary mark.

01 · PrimaryPaper edges, oxide nodes, graphite ground. The default everywhere.
02 · ReversedOn paper or any light ground. Print, light mode, documents.
03 · KnockoutOne colour on oxide. The app icon, decals, anything where oxide is the surface.
04 · One colourNodes become open rings so the points survive without a second colour. Embossing, engraving, single-plate print.
05 · ReductionBelow 24 px. Nodes dropped, stroke stepped up. The G survives; the points don’t.
06 · PlottedThe animated mark. The route travels at a constant rate and each node lands as the line reaches it. Loading, onboarding, a title card — never in place of the static mark.
Misuse — all of it fatal

Any node diameter other than 1.7t. Any node colour other than oxide or the edge colour. A cyan node. A rounded lattice. The aperture reduced below 3u. The mark rotated, sheared, outlined, given a gradient, or set inside a container shape. The wordmark set in any face other than Geologica.

07LockupsGRF-M-04

Two lockups and how they work.

Horizontal — the defaultWordmark cap height equals the mark’s lattice height. The gap is 4 lattice units, measured from the outer node edge. Use everywhere except square formats.
Stacked — square formats onlyAvatars, a stamped case, a pin. Never in running layout.

Minimum sizes

Horizontal lockup: 24 mm wide in print, 120 px on screen. Below that the wordmark closes up and you should be using the mark alone.

Mark alone: 8 mm in print, 24 px on screen. Below 24 px switch to the reduction alternate — a different file, not a scaled one.

Never

Don’t rebuild the lockup by typing GRAFFS next to the mark. The supplied files have the wordmark outlined at the correct weight, tracking and gap. Typing it will get all three wrong.

Working tints

Panel #11161B · rules #2A343B and #1E262C · soft ink #93A1AB · oxide-on-wash #EC7A55, for oxide type over a graphite panel where #D9552F drops below 4.5:1.

Contrast

Paper on graphite is 15.8:1. Soft ink on graphite is 7.4:1. Slate is for rules and disabled states only — at 3.2:1 it must never carry body copy.

Proportion

Graphite holds roughly 85% of any surface, paper and soft ink the next 12%, cyan and oxide the remaining 3%. If orange is the first thing you see on a quiet screen, something’s wrong.

09The anomalyGRF-BD-04

An anomaly is a point that has left the lattice.

Every point in this identity sits on a lattice intersection. That discipline exists so that one thing can break it. The brand needs no separate warning language, because deviation is already legible against a system this regular — which is the whole reason to build one.

Off-lattice pointThe offset is dimensioned in lattice units, never called “high”.
The windowThe interval that moved, with its duration across the top.
DivergenceObserved against baseline, the gap hatched rather than filled.
The breakAn absence, not a reading. Oxide marks the gap, never the surviving edges.
The rule this settles

Oxide appearing on a surface means a point is off its lattice, right now. On anything that reports — a console, a chart, a status page — it arrives when a point deviates and leaves when the point returns. On anything that reports nothing — an icon, a cover, a decal, a booth wall — it can be permanent and can fill the ground. The division isn’t a list of exceptions; it’s one question about what the surface is for.

What it buys: a console where orange is temporary is a console an operator can trust. Screens go quiet when the fleet is healthy, and an engineer walking past a wall display reads four hundred assets from across the room. Put orange on a button and you’ve taught them to ignore the one colour that matters.

10TypographyGRF-BD-02

Two faces. Three weights. Assigned by size, never by emphasis.

Geologica — language
Cooling system anomaly

A technical grotesque drawn for data-dense interfaces: sharpened terminals, tight apertures, a large x-height that holds at 11 px on a dark ground. Its angular terminals rhyme with a mark built from straight segments — it reads as specified equipment, not a brand choice.

Why oxide is the default ground

Oxide is the colour of first contact; graphite is the colour of use. An app icon is the thing you meet before you’ve used anything, and it reports nothing — so it can be fully oxide. It also gives Graffs the only warm icon in a category of blue ones.

Size

The mark occupies 59% of the canvas — large enough that at 40 pt, the smallest iOS renders, the nodes still read as separate points, and small enough that the corners never crowd the squircle mask.

Delivery

Two layered 1024 SVGs for Icon Composer — edges behind, nodes in front, so specular highlights catch the points first. An asset catalog with all three appearances is supplied as a fallback. Never add the wordmark: GRAFFS is unreadable below about 120 pt.

12PowerPoint templateGRF-P-01

Thirteen layouts, built on the same system.

The deck runs on three grounds. Paper and graphite alternate so that no two consecutive slides share a ground — which is what stops a thirteen-slide deck flattening into one long surface. Oxide is reserved for section breaks, the only slide type that reports nothing and so the only one permitted the whole ground.

Charts are native

Every chart is a real PowerPoint object, editable in Chart Data. Never paste a screenshot of a chart — it can’t be corrected, resized or read by anyone who needs the numbers.

Oxide is never decoration

The eyebrow label and the node motif carry it by convention, on every slide. Beyond those two it appears only on a value that actually breached — never a heading, never a bullet, never a chart series that did nothing unusual.

Every slide has notes

Speaker notes on each layout explain what it’s for and where its limits are — four stats maximum on the stat row, forty-five words per column on the two-column.

13MascotGRF-BD-06

A face for the agent, if it earns one.

Graffs ships agents that act on their own, and software that acts on its own is easier to trust when it has a presence. The risk is equal and opposite: a mascot is the fastest way to undo an identity this restrained. So the mascot is the smallest thing that could work: the node eye, a single lattice node with a pupil knocked out of it. Not a character beside the identity, but one of its own points, given somewhere to look.

It adds nothing

A lattice node with a pupil knocked out of it. No new shape, no new colour — only a use.

It can’t get cute

No face to add a mouth to, no body to draw badly. The failure mode of every mascot is closed off by construction.

It survives anywhere

One node reads at 16 px, as an avatar, on a sticker. Nothing else considered holds together that far down.

What the node eye does

It’s ink at rest, which leaves oxide free to mean what it means everywhere else — the node only turns when something has left its lattice. These are running; the timings that govern them are in section 15.

At restThe eye looks around, ready for the next directive.
ScanningThe node thins into an oxide edge and sweeps the field.
FoundThe node grows an edge above itself — an exclamation point.
DispatchedThe eye travels, looking the way it’s going, a cyan edge behind it.
ClearedThe edges close into a check. The point is back on its lattice.
Where it goes

It belongs anywhere the product isn’t reporting — onboarding, empty states, loading, an avatar, a sticker. Never on a console, and never in place of the mark.

14NamingGRF-BD-09

If it earns a name, it earns one of these.

The mascot stands for an agent — something handed an instruction that then goes and acts on it unwatched. So a name that only describes the drawing is decoration; this one has to say something about acting. It also has to be a component name, what you call this element when you specify it, the way a system says the caret — not a christening. A named thing is a character, and a character is something people want to draw, dress and give a birthday.

AyeRecommended
What the agent says
The reading

You don’t say aye to a question. You say it to an order — it’s the word that accepts a task you’ll then carry out unsupervised, which is exactly the handoff Graffs asks an operator to make. And an aye is consent, given by something that could have refused. A system that can only comply is a script, not an agent.

Where it sits

It’s the beat the states skip: Found, then a silent jump to Dispatched. Aye is the word in that gap — understood, and going. It’s also entered, not just spoken. The ayes have it is a counted affirmative, which is the accountability half of being allowed to act alone.

What it costs

Aye, eye and I are one sound. Contained, because the mascot never appears on a surface that reports, so the name is never in a sentence beside a reading.

Datum
What it answers to
The reading

Something permitted to act unwatched needs a fixed thing to be checked against; autonomy without a reference is just motion. A datum is the reference feature every measurement is taken from — the agreed ground that makes an independent action verifiable after the fact.

Where it sits

It makes the anomaly rule literal: an off-lattice point is a departure from datum, the sentence the operator would write anyway. The agent states its judgement in the plant engineer’s own vocabulary rather than the software’s.

What it costs

It names the ground, not the actor. A datum doesn’t act — it’s what action is judged against, which is close to the opposite of what a mascot is for.

Recommendation

Aye. It names the moment the product exists for: an instruction accepted by something that will now go and carry it out alone, and answer for it afterwards. Datum names the ground that action is judged against — true, useful, and not a presence. Take it instead if the product voice turns out strictly technical: no onboarding copy, no empty states, agents that only emit readings. Either way it’s a component name, and either way it wants a trademark search before it ships.

15MotionGRF-BD-07

Motion is a readout, not a performance.

The mascot moves the way the product reads. Colour steps — a state is discrete, and ink doesn’t fade into oxide any more than a reading is half-breached. Length travels — a node and an edge are the same primitive at two lengths, so the mascot never changes shape, only how far one thing reaches. The only weight in the system is the bounce, and it appears in one state: the agent already on its way somewhere.

PropertyDurationCurveWhy
Colour0 mssteppedA state is discrete. Ink doesn’t fade into oxide; it’s one or the other.
Length180 msease-outA node and an edge are one primitive at two lengths — the found bar is the node’s own rect, at the node’s radius, grown to 40. Growing it is the only morph.
Sweep1.6 sease-in-outThe scan. Fast enough to read as searching, slow enough to follow.
Idle scan3.2 sease-in-outThe eye at rest. Alert, never darting.
Bounce1.15 sease-out / ease-inUp decelerating, down accelerating. The only weight in the system, and only in transit.
Reduced motion

Every animated file honours prefers-reduced-motion by holding its final frame rather than looping. An operator who has asked their machine to stop moving things has asked for a reason, and a mascot isn’t the exception.

Start here

1. Install the fonts in 05-fonts.
2. Read this document.
3. Open the PowerPoint template.
4. Keep this where the next designer will find it.

File choice

SVG for anything that scales — web, print, signage, laser, embroidery. PNG only where SVG isn’t accepted. Never re-export a PNG from a smaller PNG.

If in doubt

Primary mark, graphite ground, Geologica Regular, and no orange. That combination is never wrong, and it’s most of the identity.

17The siteGRF-W-01

The identity, under load.

Everything above is a rule until something is built with it. The product marketing site is the first surface where the whole system carries weight at once — the lockup at 22 px in a nav, Geologica at display size, Azeret Mono on every value, and oxide spent on exactly one point in four hundred.

Oxide under load

Four hundred assets on one screen and a single orange point. A rule that survives a fleet view survives anywhere.

The node eye, running

Aye plays all five states in the agent loop, on the timings in section 15 — the same files this document uses, in /mascot.

Reversed on demand

A toggle in the footer swaps the page to the paper ground — alternate 02, one token set, no second palette.
